intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene (607429) on chromosome 10p12.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 defect has been described in three patients from two families 6, 7 carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1).
checks.explanation: Homozygous and compound heterozygous PDSS1 variants cause CoQ10 deficiency.

checks.claim: The PDSS1 gene is located on chromosome 10p12.
checks.evidence_quote: A genome-wide search for homozygosity in family 1 identified a region of chromosome 10 encompassing the gene prenyldiphosphate synthase, subunit 1 (PDSS1)
checks.explanation: The paper places PDSS1 on chromosome 10. The 10p12 band is standard nomenclature added to that location.

paragraphs.text: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is an autosomal recessive disorder of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) biosynthesis caused by mutation in the PDSS1 gene. Reported features include bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, optic atrophy with reduced vision, mild intellectual disability or developmental delay, and cardiac involvement such as valvulopathy, pulmonary hypertension or heart failure. Disease severity ranged from a progressive multisystem disorder in infancy that ended in death in early childhood to survival into adolescence.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is an autosomal recessive disorder of coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis caused by mutation in the PDSS1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We have identified 2 novel inborn errors of CoQ10 biosynthesis in 2 distinct families.
checks.explanation: The paper supports a CoQ10 biosynthesis defect caused by a homozygous PDSS1 mutation. It does not explicitly call the disorder autosomal recessive.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) reported 2 sisters born to consanguineous Egyptian parents. The proband (II:1), a 16-year-old girl born after an uneventful pregnancy, had severe language delay in early childhood. At age 4 years she was found to have profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, which was treated with an externally powered prosthesis. She also had difficulty with verbal comprehension, mild intellectual disability, and progressive visual loss. Visual acuity was 1/10 in both eyes, and she had red-green dyschromatopsia without a relative afferent pupillary defect. She had optic atrophy, mainly in the inferior temporal sector. Visual evoked potentials showed increased latency and reduced amplitude of P100, and optical coherence tomography showed reduced thickness of the retinal nerve fiber layer. Other findings were diffuse mild muscle weakness and mild postural tremor of the upper limbs. Brain MRI was normal. Cardiac evaluation showed a dysplastic mitral valve with moderate insufficiency, tricuspid insufficiency, an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 40 mmHg, and a moderately dilated left atrium. She did not have lactic acidosis, macrocephaly, peripheral neuropathy, nephrotic syndrome or failure to thrive. Her younger affected sister (II:4) also had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. At age 6 years she developed decreased visual acuity, and ophthalmologic examination showed optic atrophy with bilateral pallor of the optic nerve head in the temporal sector, as well as divergent strabismus. She had mild intellectual disability and muscular involvement. She did not have cardiac valvulopathy, lactic acidosis, macrocephaly, peripheral neuropathy or nephrotic syndrome. Nardecchia et al. (2021) noted that in PDSS1 deficiency, sensorineural deafness appeared to precede optic atrophy, unlike in OPA1 and OPA3 defects. They proposed adding PDSS1 deficiency to the differential diagnosis of optic atrophy with sensorineural deafness.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) reported a boy who presented at age 5 months with failure to thrive, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, bilateral hearing impairment, pulmonary hypertension, livedo reticularis and distal phalangeal erythema. Laboratory tests showed anemia, lactic acidosis, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, tricarboxylic aciduria and decreased CoQ10 levels in lymphocytes. Brain imaging at 12 months showed mild cerebral atrophy. He went on to develop a progressive multisystem disorder with severe developmental delay, pyramidal dysfunction, seizures, tremor, optic atrophy, nystagmus, severe visual and hearing impairment, cystic white matter change and chronic heart failure. He died at age 3 years.

paragraphs.text: Vasta et al. (2012) performed targeted next-generation sequencing of the exons of 908 known and candidate nuclear genes in 26 patients with known or suspected mitochondrial disorders. None of the 18 patients with abnormal respiratory chain complex activities had defects in respiratory chain complex subunits or assembly factors. paragraphs.text: In a family with CoQ10 deficiency (family 1), Mollet et al. (2007) found a homozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene that resulted in an asp308-to-glu (D308E) substitution at a conserved amino acid. The mutation was identified by sequencing PDSS1 within a region of homozygosity on chromosome 10. Quinone-dependent OXPHOS activities were in the range of the lowest control values, while OXPHOS enzyme activities were normal. Yeast Deltacoq1 cells transformed with the mutant yeast COQ1 gene grew poorly on respiratory medium.
